claims.text: Increasing the post-deposition annealing temperature promotes formation of a coherent, adherent oxide tribofilm on FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
The oxide tribofilm shields the coating's near-surface microstructure from cyclic shear stresses during high-temperature sliding.
Formation of a protective oxide layer reduces wear during elevated-temperature sliding in air.
The oxide tribofilm limits microscopic plastic deformation in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Atmospheric annealing at 600, 750, or 900 °C can deliberately promote oxide tribofilm formation.
The relevant operating regime is repeated cyclic sliding in air at temperatures of at least 600 °C.
A near-surface oxide or spinel tribofilm stabilizes grain boundaries.
A near-surface oxide or spinel tribofilm limits dislocation motion.
The protective oxide tribofilm reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and sliding shear stress.
Reduced contact and shear inhibit dynamic recrystallization and dislocation pile-ups.
Compared with an unannealed coating, an annealed FeNiCrCoCu coating with a well-developed oxide layer will have a lower wear rate.
Compared with an unannealed coating, an annealed FeNiCrCoCu coating with a well-developed oxide layer will have a lower coefficient of friction.
Compared with an unannealed coating, an annealed FeNiCrCoCu coating with a well-developed oxide layer will show less subsurface plastic deformation.
Oxide formation is thermodynamically favored during sliding at or above 600 °C in oxidizing environments.
The predicted protection may not occur in inert atmospheres or at substantially lower temperatures.
Annealing-induced grain coarsening may compete with oxide-film protection and alter the magnitude of the wear and deformation response.

The hypothesis is falsified if verified enhancement of the oxide tribofilm produces no statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and microscopic plastic deformation, or worsens wear performance relative to the unannealed baseline.
